findings: "an insurer that covers about four hundred yards" -> "an insurer that covers about four hundred livery yards" (passage, para 2, sentence 1)
"A number for it is more than these readings will carry" -> "I couldn’t put a number on it; these readings won’t carry that" (passage, para 2, Pallenmoor’s quotation, second sentence)
justification: Native read-aloud of all five layers. The prose is genuine BrE equestrian/science journalism throughout (indoor school, the long side, went down nine years ago, firm enough to lean a spade on, ride deep) and no comma splice, no wrong-tense sequence and no un-English collocation surfaced; the comma-splice heuristic returned zero hits in this unit. Two places make a native reader stumble. "covers about four hundred yards" lands on the canonical distance idiom before the stable-yard sense arrives, and the sense is only settled a paragraph later at "the yards with good records". And Pallenmoor’s second quoted sentence is written, not spoken: the inversion "A number for it is more than these readings will carry" is a writer’s construction placed inside speech marks; his other two sentences read as real talk, which makes the middle one stand out. Neither is a correctness fault, so flag rather than kill.

findings: "the blend under the sand isn’t the same from one supplier to the next" -> "the blend in the sand isn’t the same from one supplier to the next" (passage, para 2, Pallenmoor’s quotation)
"though not in the way the yard meant it" -> "though not in the way the yard meant" (passage, para 3, sentence 4)
justification: Systematic class-by-class sweep. Misquotation: every curly-quoted span in all five rationales was extracted and tested for membership in the passage after normalising quotes, dashes and whitespace - 20 of 20 spans are verbatim, no near-miss, no paraphrase inside quotation marks. Countability (fibre, sand, wax as mass nouns; grids, tines, cores as counts), articles, tense/aspect (have been saying, has been back, had been sorting, had not been turned), negative polarity (hardly any licensed by hardly; not with any surface licensed by not), relative pronouns (that for insurer/yards/ones, who never used of a non-person), zero relatives (the distance the warm floor needed, the wax he brought up, records he would trust - every one has a gap), mixed comparisons (distance vs distance, gap vs gap, wax vs wax, worth more than they are) and register all pass; no project-management or in-terms drift. Two residuals. The quoted "blend under the sand" contradicts the passage’s own build - the wax is "coated in wax" onto grains "mixed through with chopped fibre", and what is actually under the sand is "a membrane and crushed stone". And "not in the way the yard meant it" leaves "it" without a clean antecedent (the machine, or the blame?); the sentence is cleaner without the pronoun. Rationale substance is otherwise correct: harrowing lifts fibre, fibre keeps sand from packing, hoof loading packed the unturned eighty millimetres - all stated in the right direction.

findings: "this room is not interrupting anything, it is failing to start" -> "this room is not interrupting anything; it is failing to start" (rationale, Gap (2), the sentence on break in)
"it is not the same sound the recorder got" -> "it is not the same sound the recorder player got" (passage, para 4, sentence 3)
justification: Native read-aloud of all five layers. The essay itself is very clean spoken-thought English - the asyndetic series "No one has agreed to anything, there is no conductor to watch, and yet two hundred people find the same half-second" is a legitimate comma-joined series, not a splice, and "a negotiation about how long is decent" is a well-formed embedded question with "how long" as subject, so no inversion is missing. The cloze frames all read naturally with their keys in place, and the two duration figures (the same half-second, about a fifth of a second) are consistent rather than competing, the finer spread sitting inside the coarser window. Two stumbles. The rationale for Gap (2) contains a real comma splice, and a splice inside a text whose job is to teach English is the wrong place for one. And the passage moves "the recorder" from the instrument ("before the recorder has stopped") to the performer ("the sound the recorder got") without warning, which is native metonymy but leaves an ELF reader a live second reading - a recording device - in a sentence that Gap (5) depends on.

findings: "and English pairs it with someone or over something" -> "and English pairs it with a person (a bargain with someone) or with a thing (a bargain over something)" (rationale, Gap (3), the bargain sentence)
"A bargain is the terms two sides have already struck" -> "A bargain is the set of terms two sides have already struck" (rationale, Gap (3))
justification: Systematic class-by-class sweep plus the cloze-specific checks. Misquotation: all 6 curly-quoted spans across the five rationales tested mechanically for membership in the passage - 6 of 6 verbatim. Cloze integrity: gap 1 is four sentence-initial adverbs (Hence/Rather/Equally/Elsewhere), gap 2 four bare verbs each of which forms a real phrasal verb with in (join/cut/fall/break), gap 3 four singular abstract nouns from one commercial-social stock, gap 4 four adjectives, gap 5 four -ly adverbs; every gap is single-word-class, and in every gap exactly one option is idiomatic in context, the other three being real English that fails on sense or collocation rather than on grammar. Preposition calques, countability, false friends, articles, tense/aspect, unlicensed NPIs, who-for-non-person, gapless zero relatives, over-reaching pronouns, mixed comparisons and register drift: none found. Two residuals, both in the Gap (3) rationale and both where it is teaching prepositions. "English pairs it with someone or over something" parses on a first pass as "pairs it with [someone or over something]", which is exactly the confusion the sentence exists to remove; the metalinguistic prepositions need to be marked. And "A bargain is the terms" puts a singular subject against a plural complement in the same breath. Substance is otherwise right: fall in is genuinely the marching sense, break in and cut in are genuinely interruption senses, and outspoken genuinely applies to people and views and not to a noise.

Native read-aloud of all five layers. Compressed hospital reportage and it holds: "Carriers drop out of the wall into a padded bin, one a minute", "Between stations the trace barely moved", "a porter walks those down" all read as written by a native. Ashvenor’s speech reads as speech rather than as composed prose - a short deictic opener ("That pink is haemoglobin, from the cells"), a contracted causal chain ("They’ve burst on the way over"), a first-person hedge ("the number I’d report") and a genuine spoken cleft ("It’s the stop at the far end that does it") - which is the single hardest thing to get right in this format. No comma splice (heuristic returned zero hits in this unit), no garden path, no wrong-register word. "The loop runs at the speed it always has" and "What changed is the bins" are both within native range - the bare has pro-form is standard, and the singular copula before a plural pseudo-cleft complement is attested and is echoed consistently in the rationale ("What changed was the bins"). Nothing to report.

Systematic class-by-class sweep. Misquotation: all 7 curly-quoted spans in the single rationale extracted and tested mechanically for membership in the passage - 7 of 7 verbatim, including the three that quote whole sentences and the two that quote inside Ashvenor’s speech. Mechanism direction, the class most likely to fail here, is right in both halves and is stated explicitly: potassium is intracellular, the cells burst, the potassium therefore passes out into the plasma, and the reported figure comes out too high rather than too low; and the pink is haemoglobin released from the cells, not something present beforehand. The rationale even names the inversion risk and closes it. Also correct: whole blood is red throughout and the pink is visible only post-centrifugation, which is what makes option B’s ward reading impossible; and the blood-gas route is given the way the passage gives it. Preposition use is BrE-idiomatic and uncalqued (round the loop, taped into a carrier, holds a spun tube to the window, down by about half). Countability (blood gases plural as clinical usage, rejects a plural count), articles, tense/aspect (present scene with past-perfect-free past insets; "has never gone" for a standing practice), NPIs (Nothing shows, never gone - all licensed), relative pronouns, zero relatives with gaps, pronoun reach (they/their attaches to "the cells", the nearest and only plausible antecedent; "sent it round the loop" attaches to the carrier), mixed comparisons ("higher than the patient’s" is number against number by ordinary possessive ellipsis) and register: all clean. Nothing to report.

findings: "The letters run to March, over a gate and some stones" -> "The letters, over a gate and some stones, run to March" (passage, sentence 4)
justification: Native read-aloud of all five layers. The period register is right and unforced - thorn bank, cut from above and cleaned from below, laid, the enclosure, deposited plan, chained and pegged, no land was taken - and "attorney" is the correct English term for 1845, before the 1873 merger into solicitors, so it is period-accurate rather than an Americanism. The archival present of "The letters run to March" against the surrounding past is standard history writing, and the past perfects (had never been in dispute, had stood so, had chained and pegged) sequence correctly against the 1845 anchor. No comma splice (heuristic returned zero hits), no un-English collocation, no quoted speech at all to go wrong. One stumble: "The letters run to March, over a gate and some stones" is a garden path, because "run" plus "over" is a strong collocation and only the short intervening "to March," holds them apart, so a reader briefly gets letters running over a gate before the modifier reattaches to "letters".

findings: "but the passage names the man who enclosed it, and he acted for the neighbour" -> "but the passage says whose attorney enclosed it, and he acted for the neighbour" (rationale, option A rebuttal)
justification: Systematic class-by-class sweep. Misquotation: all 3 curly-quoted spans in the rationale extracted and tested mechanically for membership in the passage - 3 of 3 verbatim, including the two landmark phrases the key turns on ("from the stone gap down to the lane" and "along the bank, from the stone gap to the lane end"), whose near-identity is the whole inference and which had to be exactly right. Chronology and substance check out: November 1845 claim, "the previous October" correctly recovered by the rationale as the month before, letters to March 1846, February offer, scheme abandoned autumn 1846, thorn laid again 1851 - and the six-year gap from 1839 is correctly characterised as an ordinary point in a laying cycle rather than neglect, which the passage’s own 1839-to-1851 interval supports. Preposition calques, countability (timber as mass), articles, tense/aspect, NPIs (never, no land, never fell due - all licensed), relative pronouns (who only of persons: a man who wants a hedge, the man who enclosed it), zero relatives with gaps (the ground the surveyor had pegged out, the ending a pegged railway line usually has, what he was being asked for), pronoun reach (one/the other bound to the two farms), mixed comparisons and register: none found. One residual: the option A rebuttal is about attribution, and it says the passage "names the man who enclosed it" when the passage never gives him a name - he is only "The neighbour’s attorney", while Ruddiforth is the one party who is actually named. A learner sent looking for a name will not find one.
